chapter: Cee Pee Johnson, Hampton and the Navy band
title: Cee Pee Johnson's band and the Rum Boogie on Highland
summary: After Hite in 1939 Royal joined Cee Pee Johnson's novelty band, which a Chili Bowl owner hired away for his Hollywood club.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: So, you were with Les Hite until 1939. (inaudible).

About 1939, then we went to -- I went with a swinging little band out here, real fun band called Cee Pee Johnson, and it was a real fun band. We had arrangements -- it was a copy band, only it was a small band. So, we copied

big band arrangements. We'd play everything that Jimmie Lunceford ever played and we'd play everything that Duke ever played or anybody that ever made anything good and on top of that, we had things that we did that nobody else did. Like we had parodies on "Poor Butterfly," like we had called it "The Big Pat Butterfly," you know, and we'd sing it with little commutations [sic] "That commutations like that. A Chick was high, like a big fat butterfly," and things, you know, and a real fun band and we were the hottest thing in Hollywood around 1939, early '40 era.
We opened a place out on Highland for this fella that -- guy by the name of Art Wizzen (PHONETIC), that owned the -- a whole string of things called the Chili Bowls out here, years ago.

Well, he was also the -- yeah, well, he's the one that owned all the Chili Bowls, so he opened this nightclub and he stole this band, See Pee C.P. Johnson's band from a club down on -- called the Paradise Club -- on Main Street, downtown Los Angeles. So, he give us about 15, $20 more a week. So, we went to Hollywood.
Yeah, apiece, you know. We went to Hollywood, big time. And we had fun.
Oh, right near Beverly. Yeah, it was
Oh, (inaudible). I've heard the name, yeah.

Well, it was first called something else and then it became the Rum Boogie. Had very, very good line of show girls and good acts and everything. That was first-class entertainment. We had good people used to come in there.
